definitions.definition: The specific moment when something breaks or changes dramatically.
definitions.example: Like the exact second a glass shatters when dropped.

definitions.definition: A measure of how different the words and phrases used by Democrats and Republicans are from each other.
definitions.example: If Democrats always say 'climate change' and Republicans always say 'climate hoax,' that shows high distinctiveness.

definitions.definition: Completely separate ways of talking about and understanding the world, as if living in different realities.
definitions.example: Like one person speaking English and another speaking Spanish, but about politics.

definitions.definition: Coming after or as a result of something else, not the cause.
definitions.example: If your grades are downstream of studying, then studying causes good grades, not the other way around.

definitions.definition: Coming before or being the cause of something else.
definitions.example: The source of a river is upstream from the mouth.

definitions.definition: A single identity (like being a Democrat or Republican) that now predicts almost everything about a person—where they live, who they marry, what they buy, and what they believe.
definitions.example: In the past, being a Democrat only told you how someone voted; now it might tell you what car they drive and what TV shows they watch.

definitions.definition: The process by which people group themselves into teams (like tribes) based on political labels, and then adopt all the beliefs and behaviors of that team.
definitions.example: Like sports fans who start hating the other team's colors and cheering for everything their team does, even bad calls.

definitions.definition: A moment when a trend or situation changes direction or speeds up dramatically.
definitions.example: The moment a roller coaster stops climbing and starts dropping.

definitions.definition: When local or state-level issues become part of a nationwide political fight.
definitions.example: Instead of arguing about your town's potholes, everyone argues about the president's immigration policy.

definitions.definition: Using computer programs to find patterns in large amounts of data.
definitions.example: A computer reading millions of speeches to see which words Democrats and Republicans use differently.

definitions.definition: A specific point in time that marks a change or event.
definitions.example: Like a timestamp on a video showing exactly when something happened.

definitions.definition: When two groups start using language differently, making it harder to understand each other.
definitions.example: Like how British and American English grew apart after the colonies separated.

definitions.definition: When people support their party mainly because they hate the other party, not because they love their own.
definitions.example: Voting for a candidate just because you can't stand the opponent.

definitions.definition: Made stronger or more unified.
definitions.example: Glue that dries and hardens, making pieces stick together firmly.

definitions.definition: Getting large groups of people who share an identity to take political action together.
definitions.example: Like getting all fans of a sports team to show up and cheer at the same time.

definitions.definition: A measure of how much knowing someone's opinion on one issue helps you predict their opinion on another issue.
definitions.example: If knowing someone is pro-life also tells you they are pro-gun, that's high correlation.

definitions.definition: When members of different parties vote similarly on bills, showing they agree on some things.
definitions.example: A Democrat and a Republican both voting for the same education bill.

definitions.definition: A mathematical method used to measure how liberal or conservative a member of Congress is based on their voting record.
definitions.example: A score that tells you if a senator is more like Bernie Sanders or more like Ted Cruz.

definitions.definition: Voting for candidates from different parties in the same election, like voting for a Republican for president but a Democrat for senator.
definitions.example: Choosing a Coke and a Pepsi from the same vending machine.

definitions.definition: When people dislike or distrust members of the other political party based on feelings, not just policy disagreements.
definitions.example: Feeling angry or uncomfortable around someone just because they are a Republican or Democrat.

definitions.definition: A survey tool where people rate how warm or cold they feel toward a group, from 0 (very cold/negative) to 100 (very warm/positive).
definitions.example: Rating Democrats at 10 and Republicans at 90 shows strong preference for Republicans.

definitions.definition: A deep principle in physics where certain changes to a system don't affect the physical laws, helping to unify different forces.
definitions.example: Like how rotating a chessboard doesn't change the rules of chess.

definitions.definition: The best current scientific theory that explains all known fundamental particles and forces (except gravity).
definitions.example: The periodic table of elements for the smallest building blocks of matter.

definitions.definition: When people's various identities (like religion, race, or where they live) all line up with their political party.
definitions.example: If most white evangelicals are Republicans and most urban college graduates are Democrats, that's sorting.

definitions.definition: How a person labels their own political beliefs, usually from very liberal to very conservative.
definitions.example: Calling yourself a 'moderate' or a 'strong conservative.'

definitions.definition: Treating people unfairly because of their political party, similar to racial or gender discrimination.
definitions.example: Not hiring someone because they are a Democrat or Republican.

definitions.definition: Scientific studies where researchers watch how people act in controlled situations to learn about their choices and biases.
definitions.example: Giving people money and seeing if they share more with their own party members.

definitions.definition: The strange fact that knowing someone's opinion on one issue (like taxes) perfectly predicts their opinion on unrelated issues (like abortion), which shouldn't happen if people think independently.
definitions.example: If you know someone likes chocolate ice cream, you can't normally guess if they like action movies—but in politics, you can.

definitions.definition: An unseen factor that influences multiple observed things, like a hidden cause.
definitions.example: You can't see 'hunger,' but you can see someone eating a sandwich—hunger is the latent variable.

definitions.definition: When media chooses to show extreme or unusual members of the other party, making the whole group seem more extreme than it really is.
definitions.example: A news show always interviewing the angriest, most radical Democrat, making all Democrats seem angry.

definitions.definition: A set of persuasion techniques that appeal to emotions and identity rather than logic, named after the public relations pioneer Edward Bernays.
definitions.example: An ad that makes you feel patriotic or afraid, rather than giving you facts about a product.

definitions.definition: Turned a concept or idea into a practical, measurable action or system.
definitions.example: Turning the idea of 'customer satisfaction' into a specific survey with numbered ratings.

definitions.definition: When Democrats and Republicans work together to achieve a common goal.
definitions.example: Both parties agreeing to fix a broken bridge.

definitions.definition: A tax system where people with higher incomes pay a larger percentage of their income in taxes than people with lower incomes.
definitions.example: A person earning $1 million pays 30% in taxes, while someone earning $30,000 pays 10%.

definitions.definition: When a person or group faces conflicting pressures from different parts of their identity, making a simple decision difficult.
definitions.example: A union member who is also a conservative might be torn between supporting a Democratic pro-union bill and a Republican tax cut.

definitions.definition: When almost all members of a party vote the same way, with very few crossing over to vote with the other party.
definitions.example: Every Republican votes 'yes' and every Democrat votes 'no.'

definitions.definition: A political strategy where a leader takes a position that is between the two parties' positions, to appeal to the middle.
definitions.example: A president supporting a smaller tax cut than Republicans want but a larger one than Democrats want.

definitions.definition: The tendency for people to marry someone from the same political party.
definitions.example: A Democrat marrying another Democrat instead of a Republican.

definitions.definition: When people of a certain type (like Democrats) live close together in specific areas.
definitions.example: Most Democrats living in big cities and most Republicans living in rural areas.

definitions.definition: A political movement that supports using strong military power to spread democracy and American values abroad.
definitions.example: Supporting the Iraq War to remove Saddam Hussein and establish democracy.

definitions.definition: A rise to power, influence, or popularity.
definitions.example: A new pop star's ascendancy to the top of the charts.

definitions.definition: An acronym for 'Republican In Name Only,' used to criticize Republicans who are not seen as conservative enough.
definitions.example: Calling a Republican who supports some Democratic policies a 'RINO.'

definitions.definition: The large group of Americans (about 67%) who are tired of political fighting and want compromise and practical solutions.
definitions.example: People who just want the government to fix problems without all the arguing.

definitions.definition: Focused on practical results rather than ideals or theories.
definitions.example: Choosing the cheapest way to fix a leaky pipe, even if it's not the most elegant solution.

definitions.definition: The idea that the rules and processes used to make decisions should be fair and consistent for everyone.
definitions.example: Both sides getting the same amount of time to speak in a debate.

definitions.definition: The idea that resources and benefits in a society should be shared fairly among all people.
definitions.example: Making sure that tax money is used to help both rich and poor communities.

definitions.definition: Freedom from interference by others, like the government telling you what to do.
definitions.example: The freedom to say what you want without being arrested.

definitions.definition: Freedom to achieve your potential, which may require help from others or the government.
definitions.example: The freedom to get an education even if you can't afford it, because the government provides schools.

definitions.definition: A research method where you systematically study the content of media (like TV shows or news articles) to find patterns.
definitions.example: Counting how many times each political party is mentioned on Fox News vs. MSNBC.

definitions.definition: A scientific concept where the more you are exposed to something, the stronger the effect.
definitions.example: The more hours you spend watching partisan news, the more you dislike the other party.

definitions.definition: When computer programs (like on social media) automatically choose what content to show you based on your past behavior.
definitions.example: Facebook showing you more posts from your political party because you liked one of their posts.

definitions.definition: When algorithms or media producers deliberately choose content that makes people angry, because anger keeps them watching and sharing.
definitions.example: A news website putting a shocking headline to make you click and get upset.

definitions.definition: A set of ideas from psychology that focuses on unconscious thoughts, feelings, and childhood experiences shaping behavior.
definitions.example: The idea that you might dislike someone because they remind you of a childhood bully, even if you don't realize it.

definitions.definition: The practice of managing how an organization or person is perceived by the public, often through media and communication.
definitions.example: A company hiring someone to make sure news stories about them are positive.

definitions.definition: Sending very specific messages to very small groups of people based on detailed data about them.
definitions.example: A campaign sending an ad about gun rights only to people who have bought hunting gear.

definitions.definition: When computer programs tailor content (like ads or news) to each individual user based on their data.
definitions.example: Netflix suggesting movies based on what you've watched before.

definitions.definition: Doing something on a very large scale using computers and data, not just human effort.
definitions.example: Sending millions of personalized emails automatically, instead of writing each one by hand.

definitions.definition: Pieces of data that stand in for or hint at a person's identity, like their buying habits suggesting their political views.
definitions.example: If you buy a lot of hunting gear, a computer might guess you are a conservative.

definitions.definition: Creating a detailed picture of someone's personality, values, and motivations based on data.
definitions.example: Using your Facebook likes to guess if you are open-minded or conscientious.

definitions.definition: Studying the relationships and connections between people to understand how information or influence spreads.
definitions.example: Mapping who talks to whom on Twitter to find the most influential users.

definitions.definition: Predicting how a piece of information will spread from person to person, like a chain reaction.
definitions.example: Guessing that a funny video will go viral because it's shared by popular accounts.

definitions.definition: A method of comparing two versions of something (like an ad or a webpage) to see which one works better.
definitions.example: Showing half of users a blue button and half a red button to see which gets more clicks.

definitions.definition: A loop where an effect makes its own cause stronger, leading to more of the same effect.
definitions.example: The more you practice guitar, the better you get, which makes you want to practice more.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; things tend to become more disordered over time.
definitions.example: Your room naturally gets messier over time unless you clean it.

definitions.definition: The event that starts a process or chain reaction.
definitions.example: A spark that starts a forest fire.

definitions.definition: A group of people who share common interests but are not yet organized or acting together.
definitions.example: All the people who prefer vanilla ice cream but haven't formed a 'Vanilla Lovers' club.'

definitions.definition: Solutions to political problems that involve more participation, information, or discussion among citizens.
definitions.example: Holding more town hall meetings so people can talk directly to their representatives.

definitions.definition: When an action has the opposite effect of what was intended.
definitions.example: Trying to put out a fire with gasoline.

definitions.definition: To go beyond or rise above a limit or category.
definitions.example: A friendship that transcends political differences.

definitions.definition: Strong loyalty to one's own group (like a political party) combined with hostility toward other groups.
definitions.example: Cheering for your sports team and booing the other team, even when they do something
